summary: Field Memory is a bilingual web app that helps corn, soybean, and wheat farmers in the U.S. Midwest compare crop-rotation options for future seasons. A season does not end at harvest: some fungi and pests overwinter in crop residue or soil, while dry years affect estimated soil-water availability. Using NASA POWER climate data (hourly since 2001 and daily since 1981), Field Memory assesses weather favorability for selected crop problems where climate rules are available and estimates crop water-stress days with a simplified FAO-56 soil-water balance. Combined with USDA SSURGO soil information and rules from university extension services, it compares rotations side by side: how each may affect selected crop problems, estimated “thirsty days,” and other trade-offs. Results refer to the selected location or regional reference point; they do not predict infection or prescribe a single answer. The app explains whether each result comes from a sourced agronomic rule, a climate-based adjustment, an assumption, or the farmer’s observations, so farmers and their advisors can explore the evidence and make their own decisions.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Field Memory answers one question for a Midwest farmer: what should I plant next year? In four steps the farmer (1) picks the field location and current crop, (2) sees what the past season left in the field, (3) compares rotations side by side, and (4) gets a one-page summary to discuss with an advisor.

HOW IT WORKS

- NASA POWER (MERRA-2 / GEOS-IT): hourly temperature and relative humidity since 2001 are used to count, every year, the days that were favorable for each disease during its susceptible window (for example, long humid spells for gray leaf spot). Daily rain and temperature since 1981 drive an FAO-56 soil-water balance (Hargreaves reference evapotranspiration, crop coefficients by month) that counts "thirsty days": days in the crop season when the soil has given up about half of the water the roots can reach.

- USDA NRCS SSURGO (Soil Data Access): the soil texture at the reference point and a 2 x 2 km soil map, so the farmer can tap where the field actually is.

- University extension rules: where each problem survives the winter and how many years without its host crop it needs to decline.

THE FRAMEWORK

Each problem is classified by where it survives: in the soil for years (white mold), in surface residue (gray leaf spot, tar spot), in the soil tied to one crop (corn rootworm), or not in the field at all, arriving on the wind (southern rust). That single idea explains what a rotation can and cannot do, and it is shown to the farmer in plain language.

EXAMPLE

Central Iowa, corn after corn: two problems at high attention. Switching to corn-soybean-wheat brings high-attention problems from 2 to 0 and average thirsty days per season from about 50 to 41, at the cost of needing a wheat buyer and adding a soybean disease to watch. The 25-year record also shows 1988, 2012 and 2023 as the driest seasons for corn at this site, matching known droughts.

WHY IT CAN BE TRUSTED

- Levels are relative comparisons, not infection probabilities, and the app says so.

- Each level is broken down: base level from the rotation rule, plus or minus one level from the site's climate history, plus or minus one level from what the farmer saw.

- Every statement is tagged by origin: NASA POWER data, USDA SSURGO data, sourced agronomic rule, or assumption. Sources, assumptions and known gaps are listed for each problem.

- Water is presented as an estimate with a sensitivity range across the soil's water-holding capacity, plus a dry-year vs. typical-year comparison. It is not a forecast.

- Scope is explicit: a pilot for corn, soybean and wheat in the U.S. Midwest.

IMPACT

Rotation is one of the cheapest tools a farmer has against overwintering diseases and drought stress, but the evidence is usually scattered and generic. Field Memory turns 25+ years of NASA climate records for the farmer's own location into a side-by-side comparison anyone can read on a phone, in English or Spanish.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a risk score or a black-box recommendation, the app is built around "field memory": what each season leaves behind in the field, and which rotation erases it. It keeps every number traceable to its source.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy), plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with no framework, SVG graphics, hosted on Vercel. 46 automated tests. NASA POWER and SSURGO responses are cached; closed years are stored permanently and the current provisional year refreshes every few days.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Farmers with little technical background, mobile use outdoors, plain language, accessibility (contrast, keyboard, reduced motion), bilingual content, privacy (only coordinates leave the browser, to NASA and USDA), image licensing, and honest limits: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide, so the tool describes the area, not the exact field.

AI DISCLOSURE

AI assistants (Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT) helped write code and text under human review. The crop illustrations, home-page graphic and logo were generated with AI and carry a visible "generated by AI" mark; the app icon is hand-made. All calculations come from the code and the cited data, not from an AI model.
